title: Oregon Man Faces Citizenship Revocation After Decades-Long Identity Fraud Uncovered by Fingerprint Match
excerpt: Federal prosecutors allege Indian-born Jaswinder Singh used two identities across 23 years of immigration proceedings, evading a 1990 deportation order to eventually naturalize in 2013.
body:
• The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil denaturalization complaint against 54-year-old Jaswinder Singh of Oregon, alleging he used a second identity to obtain citizenship after being ordered deported under his original name in 1990.
  • Federal investigators matched fingerprints from both identities through a DHS digitization initiative, connecting an asylum case from 1990 to a naturalization granted in 2013.
  • Singh, a longtime Salem-area business owner and father of three, is the first person targeted for denaturalization in Oregon during the Trump administration's second term.
  • The case is part of an accelerating federal push — the DOJ filed denaturalization actions against 29 individuals in May and June alone, up from a historical average of 11 cases per year.

Federal prosecutors have filed a civil lawsuit to strip a longtime Oregon resident of his American citizenship, alleging a scheme of identity fraud that stretches back more than three decades to his first arrival in the United States.

Two Names, Two Immigration Applications

According to the complaint filed June 15 in U.S. District Court in Eugene, Jaswinder Singh — also known as Balwinder Singh — first entered the country in 1990 at San Francisco International Airport without valid travel documents. He told officers his name was Balwinder Singh, that he was born in India in 1971, and that he had purchased a Nepalese passport from a smuggler.

https://x.com/JoforOregon/status/2087230740182573346

Paroled into the country, he applied for immigration authorization in August 1990. An immigration judge denied the application that November and ordered his deportation. Singh appealed, claiming he had been arrested and beaten by Indian police over alleged involvement in Sikh separatist activities. The appeal was denied after the judge found he had failed to provide evidence corroborating government persecution.

Ordered to surrender to immigration authorities in July 1993, Singh never appeared. Instead, prosecutors allege, he submitted a second immigration application in November 1994 under the name Jaswinder Singh, providing a different date of birth and a different date of entry into the United States. An immigration judge granted this application in August 2003.

"J. Singh willfully misrepresented his identity and immigration history throughout the naturalization process."

— Immigration Services Officer, affidavit dated May 13, 2026

Singh filed for permanent residency in September 2004 and was approved without an interview in February 2008. He then submitted a naturalization application in January 2013, again certifying under penalty of perjury that he had never been ordered deported or removed. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services approved his application on June 3, 2013.

How Fingerprints Unraveled the Case

The connection between the two identities came through a Department of Homeland Security initiative to digitize paper fingerprint records from older immigration files. A laboratory analysis conducted in 2017 confirmed the fingerprints submitted under both names belonged to the same individual. Investigators also noted that Singh listed the same parents' names in both applications.

Singh told the Statesman Journal that 2017 was the year he was first stopped and questioned while traveling with his family. His attorney, Saad Ahmad, said as of mid-June they had not yet received a copy of the federal complaint.

A Community Figure Faces Denaturalization

Singh has deep roots in the Salem-Keizer area. He has owned and operated a United Market in north Salem since 2002 and co-owns Spicee Bite, a local Indian restaurant. He has three children, including two who recently graduated from university, and is part of the local Sikh community.

A USCIS spokesperson said the agency maintains "a zero-tolerance policy for anyone who lies or misrepresents themselves during the naturalization process."

Part of a Broader Federal Crackdown

The case lands in the context of a dramatically expanded federal denaturalization effort. From 1990 to 2017, an average of 11 denaturalization cases were filed annually. The current administration has accelerated the pace sharply — the DOJ announced actions against 12 individuals on May 8 and another 17 on June 8, targeting people accused of offenses ranging from identity fraud to material support for terrorism.

For Indian-origin immigrants and the broader diaspora, the case underscores how legacy immigration proceedings — even those dating back decades — can resurface through modern forensic tools. Civil denaturalization proceedings are separate from criminal prosecution and focus solely on whether citizenship was lawfully obtained. If a federal court finds Singh liable, his citizenship would be revoked, potentially leaving him subject to deportation.
nri_angle: Highlights how legacy immigration cases can resurface through modern fingerprint digitization, directly relevant to Indian-origin immigrants who may have complex early immigration histories.
author: Diaspora Desk
